title: A quantum bit that errs 5 times in a million was built from 37 noisy ones, Quantinuum says
body: On 19 October 2026 the firm Quantinuum announced, in a [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24077) posted three days earlier, a logical qubit on its 98-qubit Helios ion-trap computer that erred only about 5 times in a million rounds, [Science News reported](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/quantum-computer-megaquops-error-correction). A physical qubit is fragile: its state is a direction on a sphere, stray fields nudge it, it cannot be cloned, and measuring it to check destroys the state. So a code spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones and measures only parities, whether neighbours agree, which reveal where an error struck without revealing the data; a code of distance 7 corrects any 3 errors. At distance 3, 7 qubits erred 5.5 times in 10,000 rounds; at distance 5, 19 qubits erred 3.8 times in 100,000; at distance 7, 37 qubits erred 5 times in a million, each step dividing the error by about 12, the sign of being below threshold, where adding qubits helps rather than hurts. Google’s 2024 demonstration divided the error by about 2 per step. The result is a memory benchmark decoded after the fact, and logical gates at distance 5 still erred about 7 times in 100,000.

slides.question: Quantinuum’s logical qubit of October 2026 errs about 5 times in a million rounds. How many physical qubits make it up?
slides.explanation: 37, in a distance-7 colour code. Distance 3 took 7 qubits and erred 5.5 times in 10,000; distance 5 took 19 and erred 3.8 in 100,000. Each step cut the error by about 12.

slides.alt: Animation on dark violet: the number 5 and a triangle of 37 coloured dots, a Bloch sphere with a wobbling arrow and a crossed-out copy, parity triangles lighting up around a red dot, a log-scale ladder of errors falling from 5.5 in 10,000 to 5 in a million, bars dividing by 2 and by 12, and caveats.

slides.prompt: Protect a bit with copies and a majority vote. Get the logical error below one in a million, then try a copy that errs 60% of the time.
slides.takeaway: At 1% per copy, seven copies err less than once in a million; at 60%, every copy you add makes the vote worse. That cross-over is the threshold, and Quantinuum’s qubits sit well below it.

slides.heading: Logical errors per million rounds, by code distance
slides.note: Quantinuum, Helios, arXiv 2610.24077 (16 October 2026); a memory benchmark over 20 rounds.

slides.heading: Why not just copy the qubit?
slides.text: A classical bit can be copied three times and majority-voted. A qubit cannot be cloned, and measuring it to check destroys its state. So a code spreads one logical qubit over many physical ones and measures only parities, whether neighbours agree, which show where an error struck without revealing the data.

slides.question: What does it mean that Quantinuum’s qubits are ‘below threshold’?
options: Adding qubits to the code cuts the error
The computer runs below room temperature
Each qubit errs less than 1% of the time
slides.explanation: Below threshold, each step up in code distance divides the logical error, here by about 12; above it, more qubits would mean more errors. That is what makes scaling up worthwhile.
